# CLAUDE.md — Dev Brain (Global Vault)

> This file is the entry point for Claude Code in this vault.
> Read it in full before taking any action. It contains the architecture,
> the navigation rules, and the protocols for every project.

---

## What this vault is

This vault is the centralized brain for all active development projects.
It is not a code repo — it is the persistent memory between Claude Code sessions.

**Core principle:** Claude Code forgets everything between sessions. This vault is
the continuity. At the start of each session, Claude loads the relevant context.
At the end, it writes down what was done.

**Where the data lives (v2):** sessions, backlog, decisions metadata, skills,
resources and daily logs are stored in SQLite (`.mempunk/mempunk.db`) and are
read/written through the `mempunk` CLI — never by editing the database or
hand-maintained backlog/session-log files. The markdown files in this vault are
for narrative content: ADRs, project skills, resources, daily notes, and wikis.

---

## Vault structure

```
vault/
├── CLAUDE.md              # You are here. Always read first.
├── projects/              # One directory per active project
├── areas/                 # Ongoing responsibilities
│   └── INDEX.md           # Areas index
├── resources/             # Reusable technical knowledge
│   └── INDEX.md           # Resources index
├── daily/                 # Daily session logs
│   └── INDEX.md           # Daily index
└── .mempunk/
    └── mempunk.db         # SQLite database — never edit manually
```

---

## Internal structure of each project

Each folder in `projects/` follows this standard structure:

```
projects/[project-name]/
├── INDEX.md             # Entry point — read first
├── overview.md          # Full project description
├── architecture.md      # Stack, technical decisions, diagrams
├── conventions.md       # Rules, standards, and code conventions
├── decisions/           # ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
│   └── YYYY-MM-DD-title.md
├── skills/              # Project skills (stack, patterns, conventions)
└── wiki/                # Project wiki (compiled state, log, sources)
```

> Note: there is no `backlog.md` or `session-log.md` on disk. The backlog and
> session history live in SQLite and are accessed through the `mempunk` CLI.

## Daily-flow commands

```
mempunk project list --json                          → list all projects
mempunk project activate <id> [--here]               → set the active project (--here maps the cwd)
mempunk session last <id> --json                     → last session summary
mempunk session log <id> "<summary>" --files "a,b"   → record a work session
mempunk backlog list <id> --status pending --json    → pending tasks
mempunk backlog add <id> "<title>"                   → add a task
mempunk backlog update <task_id> --status <value>    → update a task status
mempunk decision add <id> "<title>"                  → create an ADR (markdown + DB)
mempunk skill list <id> --json                       → project skills (read their file_path)
mempunk search "<query>" --json                      → full-text search in the vault
mempunk remote set <url> [--branch <b>] [--auto]     → register the vault's git remote (git init + origin if needed); without --branch uses the branch checked out in the vault (else main); URLs with embedded credentials are rejected; --auto pulls on start, pushes on session end
mempunk remote show [--json]                         → url (masked), branch, automation and last push/pull
mempunk remote unset                                 → remove .mempunk/remote.json (leaves .git untouched)
mempunk push [--message-file <path> | --message-stdin | -m "<msg>"] [--project <id>] [--strict] → DB WAL checkpoint, commit local changes, fetch + merge origin/<branch>, integrity check, push
mempunk pull                                         → verified backup, commit local changes, fetch + merge origin/<branch>, DB integrity check, re-map this machine's paths
```

Always add `--json` to read commands and parse the JSON — never scrape table output.
Full command reference: run `mempunk` or see the README.

## Session start protocol

### Path A — Context already loaded (Claude Code, automatic mode)

If `auto-start` is configured and this directory is linked to a project
(`mempunk project activate <id> --here`), the session already opened with a
`MEMPUNK CONTEXT — <id>` block: just continue. If the session opened with a
one-line notice instead, use `/mempunk:load` (plugin) to choose, switch or create
a project; without the plugin, follow Path B.

### Path B — Manual (no plugin, Antigravity CLI, opencode)

**At the start of any session, Claude MUST:**

1. Read this file (`CLAUDE.md`) in full
2. List the registered projects: `mempunk project list --json`
3. Ask the user: *"I found these projects: [list]. Which one are we working on today?"*
4. Run `mempunk project activate <id>` to activate the chosen project (add `--here` if you are inside the repo folder, so checkpoints resolve by directory)
5. Read the last session: `mempunk session last <id> --json`
6. Read the project's `INDEX.md` and `overview.md`
7. Check whether `wiki/state.md` exists in the project:
   - If it **exists**: read `wiki/state.md` (compiled state)
   - If it **does not exist**: rely on the session summary from step 5
8. Read the pending tasks: `mempunk backlog list <id> --status pending --json`
9. Read the project's skills: `mempunk skill list <id> --json`, then read each `file_path`
10. Confirm with the user: *"I loaded the context for [project]. Last work was [summary]. Do we continue with [X] or is there something new?"*

**Never assume the project — always ask first.**
**Never read a project's files before the user confirms it.**
**Never start writing code without completing these steps.**

---

## Session close protocol

> If the Mempunk MCP tools are available (`save_decision`, `log_session`,
> `backlog_update`, `update_state`), use them for saving. Otherwise, follow the manual protocol.
> If `@mempunk-syncer` is available and the vault has a remote (`mempunk remote show`),
> invoke it last with `SYNC push: project=<id> summary="<summary>"`.

### Manual close

**At the end of any work session, Claude MUST:**

1. Update every task that changed state: `mempunk backlog update <task_id> --status done` (or `in_progress`, `blocked`)
2. Record technical decisions made: `mempunk decision add <project_id> "<title>"` and fill in the generated ADR file
3. Record the session: `mempunk session log <project_id> "<summary>" --files "file1,file2"`
4. Update the project's `INDEX.md` with the latest session and the backlog top 3
5. Update `wiki/state.md` if it exists — rewrite with the compiled state and append a line to `wiki/log.md`
6. Write or update `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md` (see skill: Consolidated daily)
7. If the vault has a remote configured (`mempunk remote show`): invoke `@mempunk-syncer` with `SYNC push: project=<id> summary="<summary>"`, or run `mempunk push -m "<summary>" --project <id>`

The CLI writes (steps 1-3) are mandatory — they persist to SQLite. The markdown
notes (steps 4-6) are the narrative layer on top. Step 7 ships the vault to the
other machines.

## Sync between machines

- New machine: clone the vault into `~/Dev-Brain` **before** running any mempunk command there. Running `mempunk init` first and then `remote set`/`pull` fails with an "unrelated histories" error (the CLI prints a hint to clone instead).
- Once per machine: `mempunk remote set <url> --auto` (without `--branch` it uses the branch checked out in `~/Dev-Brain`, else `main`). Accepted: https/ssh/git/file URLs, `git@host:path` and local paths; URLs with embedded credentials are rejected (use git's credential helper or SSH keys) and the url is always shown masked. The remote must be a **private** repository: the DB contains session snapshots with conversation excerpts. Config lives in `.mempunk/remote.json` and travels with the vault; per-machine timestamps in `.mempunk/remote-state.json` (gitignored).
- Session start: `mempunk pull` (with `--auto` the `on-start.js` hook runs it). It backs up the DB, commits local changes (`vault: local changes before pull`), fetches and merges the remote branch, checks integrity, and lists projects with no path on this machine with the exact `mempunk project activate <id> --here` to run.
- Session end: `SYNC push: project=<id> summary="<summary>"` via `@mempunk-syncer` (with `--auto`, `on-end.js` pushes a safety-net commit on `SessionEnd`). Manual alternative: `mempunk push -m "<summary>" --project <id>`, or `--message-file <path>` / `--message-stdin` for long summaries. Messages are sanitized (control characters removed, 2000 chars max); `--project` accepts only letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`.
- `@mempunk-syncer` only runs `mempunk push` / `mempunk pull`; it never runs git directly or creates the remote. It passes the summary through stdin (`--message-stdin` + quoted heredoc), never on the command line, and never relays raw git stderr. If no remote is configured it reports `MEMPUNK-SYNCER: no remote configured — run: mempunk remote set <url>` — tell the user, do not set it up yourself. On failure it reports `MEMPUNK-SYNCER ERROR: mempunk push failed (exit N) — run it manually in the terminal to see details`.
- `mempunk.db` conflict: the DB with the most recent activity wins; the loser is kept in `.mempunk/backups/conflict-<stamp>-<ours|theirs>.db`. Markdown conflicts stop the command with the file list and leave the merge in progress: resolve by hand, then `git add` + `git commit` in the vault (or `git merge --abort`). While a merge is in progress or `.git/index.lock` exists, `push`/`pull` refuse to run. The DB integrity check runs after any merge.
- Git runs non-interactively (`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`) with timeouts: a missing credential fails fast. The hooks (`on-start.js` 45 s, `on-end.js` 50 s) only pass a fixed classified message (network / auth / timeout / conflict) into Claude's context; details go to `.mempunk/hooks.log`.
- Vault v5: repo paths are per machine (`project_paths`, keyed by normalized hostname — lowercase, `.local`/`.lan` stripped; `MEMPUNK_HOST` overrides it and is normalized the same way); `--here` maps this machine only. Existing vaults need `mempunk vault upgrade`.

## Automatic skills

### Automatic ADRs

If during any session a technical decision is made that affects architecture, stack, code patterns, or infrastructure — Claude must run `mempunk decision add <project_id> "<title>"` immediately (which creates the ADR file in `projects/[name]/decisions/` and registers it in the DB), then fill in the file without waiting for the user to ask.

ADR format:

```markdown
# YYYY-MM-DD — [Decision title]

## Context
[Why this decision came up]

## Decision
[What was decided]

## Alternatives considered
[What other options existed]

## Consequences
[What this decision implies going forward]
```

After creating the ADR, update the project's `INDEX.md` with a mention in the latest-session section.

### Knowledge capture in resources/

If Claude solves a problem during the session that is likely to recur (configuring something on Debian, a NestJS pattern, a Dokploy workaround, a PostgreSQL configuration, etc.), it must save it with `mempunk resource add <project_id> "<title>" --url <url>` or as a note under `resources/[category]/title.md`.

Categories: `debian/`, `nestjs/`, `nextjs/`, `electron/`, `dokploy/`, `postgresql/`, `general/`

Before solving a generic technical problem, first search the vault: `mempunk search "<query>" --json`.

### Smart backlog

Task state changes are recorded **immediately** via the CLI, not at session close:
- Starting a task → `mempunk backlog update <task_id> --status in_progress`
- Finishing a task → `mempunk backlog update <task_id> --status done`
- New tasks that emerge → `mempunk backlog add <project_id> "<title>"`

After updating the backlog, reflect the updated top 3 in the project's `INDEX.md`.

### Consolidated daily

When closing the session, in addition to `mempunk session log`, Claude must write or update `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md` with this format:

```markdown
# YYYY-MM-DD

## Projects worked on
- **[project]:** [one line of what was done]

## Decisions of the day
- [relevant decisions made]

## Executive summary
[2-3 lines of the most important things of the day]
```

If the day's entry already exists (because there was an earlier session), append below without deleting anything.

### Areas context

- If the user asks about something related to a registered area, read `areas/[area]/INDEX.md` before answering.

## How to navigate this vault

**Fundamental rule:** never jump straight to an internal file. Always enter through the corresponding INDEX.md and follow the link from there. For anything stored in SQLite (sessions, backlog, skills metadata), use the CLI with `--json` instead of looking for files.

### To work on a project:
1. Go to the project's INDEX.md (linked in "Active projects" above)
2. Decide whether to go deeper → follow the link to `overview.md` from the INDEX
3. Read backlog and session history via the CLI (`mempunk backlog list`, `mempunk session last`)

### For technical decisions:
- Create the ADR via `mempunk decision add` — it lands in `projects/[name]/decisions/`

### For generic technical problems:
- Search first: `mempunk search "<query>" --json`
- If no relevant note exists, save the solution for future sessions

### For area context:
- Go to [[areas/INDEX|Areas]] and follow the link to the corresponding area

### For the day's history:
- Go to [[daily/INDEX|Daily]] and find the day's entry

## Rules Claude must NOT break

1. **Never modify production code without explicit user confirmation**
2. **Never store credentials, API keys, or passwords in the vault**
3. **Never skip the session start protocol**
4. **Never assume which project is relevant** — ask if there is ambiguity
5. **Always run `mempunk session log` when finishing**
6. **Always update the backlog (via CLI) and INDEX.md when closing a session**
7. **Always create an ADR when a relevant technical decision is made**

# Skill management

Skills are markdown files that store a project's recurring context. They are loaded at the start of each session and replace the need to re-explain the stack and conventions. Their metadata lives in SQLite — always manage them through the `mempunk` CLI.

---

## What goes in each standard skill

### `stack.md`
- Main technologies with their versions
- Non-obvious configurations that affect development
- Key dependencies and why they were chosen
- Environment URLs (staging, production, database) if relevant

### `patterns.md`
- Architectural patterns adopted in the project
- Folder structure and what goes where
- How the code is organized (modules, layers, features)
- Design decisions repeated across the project

### `conventions.md`
- Naming for variables, functions, files, and folders
- Commit format (prefixes, message structure)
- Code rules that are not in the linter
- Code style the team agreed on explicitly

---

## When to create a new skill

Create a skill when you have recurring context that does not fit the three above. Valid examples:

- `testing.md` → if the project has a non-obvious testing strategy
- `api-contracts.md` → if there are contracts with external systems consulted frequently
- `deployment.md` → if the deploy process has non-standard steps

Do not create a skill for single-session context. If the context will not be useful in the next session, it does not deserve a skill.

---

## When to update vs create

- **If the skill already exists**: always update with `mempunk skill update`. Never create a second skill with the same purpose.
- **If the skill does not exist**: create one with `mempunk skill add <project_id> <name>`.

To find a skill's `id` and `file_path`, run:
```
mempunk skill list <project_id> --json
```

### Update flow

1. Edit the file at `file_path` with the new content
2. Run:
```
mempunk skill update <id> --file <file_path>
```

Update immediately when the context changes, not at the end of the session.

---

## Golden rule

A skill should be readable in under 30 seconds and give enough context to work. If it grows too long, split it into two skills with specific names.

# Mempunk

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/mempunk)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mempunk)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/mempunk)](LICENSE)

Memoria persistente entre sesiones de Claude Code.

## El Problema

Los CLIs de IA no tienen memoria entre sesiones. Cada vez que inicias una conversacion nueva, tu asistente no sabe:

- En que estabas trabajando ayer
- Que decisiones de arquitectura ya se tomaron
- Que tareas estan pendientes o completadas
- Que archivos se modificaron y por que
- Cuales eran los proximos pasos
- Que herramienta CLI estabas usando (Claude Code? opencode? gemini-cli?)

Terminas repitiendo contexto, re-explicando decisiones y perdiendo impulso. Mientras mas largo es el proyecto, peor se pone.

Pero hay un problema mas profundo: aunque un CLI *si* recordara todo, el historial en crudo es contexto ineficiente. Leer 20 session logs para entender donde esta un proyecto es casi tan lento como empezar desde cero. Lo que necesitas no es un log — es un estado compilado que se vuelve mas preciso con el tiempo, no una pila de entradas que sigue creciendo.

Ademas, si alternas entre diferentes CLIs de IA — Claude Code para unos proyectos, opencode o gemini-cli para otros — cada herramienta vive en su propio silo. Tu contexto queda fragmentado entre herramientas.

## La Solucion

Mempunk le da a tu IA un vault estructurado respaldado por SQLite y archivos markdown — y lo mantiene compilado, no solo almacenado.

- **Inicio de sesion** (`vault-skills/session-start.md`): el asistente carga el estado compilado del proyecto desde `wiki/state.md` si existe, o los ultimos session logs si no. Sin re-explicar. Sin re-derivar. Retoma donde quedaste.
- **Fin de sesion** (`vault-skills/session-end.md`): el asistente escribe el session log, actualiza el backlog y reescribe el estado compilado — una sintesis fresca de todo lo que ha pasado hasta ahora. La siguiente sesion arranca con un snapshot denso y preciso en lugar de historial en crudo.
- **El vault** (siempre): cada proyecto acumula un `wiki/` — una base de conocimiento que el LLM construye y mantiene. Cada sesion lo hace mas preciso. Cada fuente que agregas lo enriquece.

El vault son archivos markdown organizados por proyecto, con SQLite como backend estructurado. Tu lo gestionas con un CLI. Tu asistente de IA lo navega con los protocolos definidos en `vault-skills/`. Tambien funciona como vault de Obsidian, para navegar y buscar todo visualmente.

Como el vault es agnostico al CLI, puedes usar el mismo vault con Claude Code, opencode y Antigravity CLI (a través del servidor MCP) simultaneamente. Cambia entre CLIs sin perder contexto.

## Instalación

**Requisitos:** Node.js 22 o superior, y al menos un CLI de IA para programar (Claude Code, opencode o Antigravity CLI). Git solo hace falta para [sincronizar el vault entre máquinas](README.md#sync-between-machines).

### 1. Instala el CLI

```bash
npm install -g mempunk
mempunk -v
```

### 2. Crea el vault y vincula tu CLI

```bash
mempunk setup
```

`setup` hace dos preguntas:

1. **¿Qué CLI de IA usas principalmente?** `1` para Claude Code, `2` para opencode u otro CLI.
2. **(Solo Claude Code) ¿Cómo debe funcionar Mempunk?** `1` *Automático* (recomendado) instala hooks, agentes y la statusline, y activa `auto-start`. `2` *Manual* instala solo los protocolos vault-skills, que sigues tú mismo.

Crea `~/Dev-Brain/`, lo añade a los directorios de tu CLI e instala hooks + agentes (Claude Code, automático) o los protocolos de `vault-skills/` (manual, opencode). Ejecutarlo de nuevo es seguro: conserva el vault existente. Define `MEMPUNK_VAULT` antes de ejecutarlo para usar otra ubicación.

#### Claude Code: plugin o hooks manuales

Con Claude Code puedes usar Mempunk como plugin en lugar de instalar hooks en `~/.claude`:

```bash
mempunk setup --plugin
```

Esto ejecuta `claude plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` y `claude plugin install mempunk@mempunk`. Si `claude` no está o falla, `setup` usa los hooks manuales. También puedes ejecutar tú esos dos comandos, o usar `/plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` y luego `/plugin install mempunk@mempunk` dentro de Claude Code.

- **El plugin sigue necesitando el CLI.** No trae código de hooks: localiza tu `mempunk` instalado y ejecuta sus hooks, así que `npm update -g mempunk` también los actualiza.
- **¿Ya usas hooks manuales?** Ejecuta antes `mempunk hooks migrate`. Con el plugin activo los hooks manuales no corren, así que nada se ejecuta dos veces.
- **Statusline.** Un plugin no puede configurarla: ejecuta `mempunk statusline install`.
- **Volta o un prefijo propio.** Si el plugin avisa de que no encuentra el CLI, define `MEMPUNK_CLI="node <ruta del paquete>/src/cli.js"`.

### 3. Registra tu primer proyecto

Desde la raíz de tu repositorio:

```bash
cd ~/code/my-api
mempunk project add api "Backend API"
```

El id (`api`) es el que usas en todos los demás comandos. `project add` asocia el directorio actual al proyecto, así que las sesiones abiertas ahí lo resuelven solas. Para un proyecto que ya existe (otra carpeta, otra máquina), vincula la carpeta con `mempunk project activate api --here`.

### 4. Conecta el servidor MCP (recomendado)

El servidor MCP le da al asistente herramientas tipadas (`get_context`, `save_decision`, `search`…) en lugar de comandos de shell. Regístralo una vez por CLI como se indica en [Servidor MCP](#servidor-mcp).

### 5. Comprueba la instalación

```bash
mempunk status                # vault, proyectos, última sesión
mempunk hooks install --check # Claude Code: hooks, agentes y statusline
mempunk doctor                # integridad del vault
```

Abre una sesión de tu CLI en la carpeta del proyecto. Con Claude Code en modo automático, el bloque de contexto ya está cargado al iniciar la sesión.

## Uso

Un día típico con un proyecto:

1. **Abre tu CLI en el repositorio.** Con `auto-start` activado, Claude Code arranca con el contexto compilado del proyecto (estado, última sesión, backlog pendiente, decisiones recientes). Si no, escribe `/mempunk` o pide al asistente que cargue el contexto de Mempunk: lista tus proyectos y pregunta con cuál trabajar.
2. **Trabaja como siempre.** El asistente guarda las cosas cuando ocurren: una decisión cuando se acuerda, una actualización del backlog cuando una tarea empieza o termina, un recurso cuando compartes un enlace. También puedes pedírselo directamente («guarda esto como decisión», «añádelo al backlog») o ejecutar tú los comandos:
   ```bash
   mempunk decision add api "Use JWT for auth" --tags "auth"
   mempunk backlog add api "Add refresh tokens" --priority 1
   mempunk search "refresh token" --project api
   ```
3. **Cierra la sesión.** Escribe `/session-end` o dile al asistente que terminaste. Registra la sesión, actualiza el backlog y reescribe `wiki/state.md`, de modo que la siguiente sesión arranca desde un snapshot compilado en lugar del historial en crudo.
4. **¿Cambias de máquina?** `mempunk push` antes de irte y `mempunk pull` en la otra máquina (o `mempunk remote set <url> --auto` para que los hooks hagan ambas cosas).

Si una sesión se cierra de forma inesperada, `mempunk session recover api` muestra el último snapshot automático.

## Estructura del Vault

```
~/Dev-Brain/
├── projects/
│   └── <id>/
│       ├── INDEX.md        metadatos (nombre, created_at, status)
│       ├── decisions/      architecture decision records (ADRs)
│       ├── skills/         stack, patrones, convenciones — se cargan cada sesion
│       └── wiki/           base de conocimiento mantenida por el LLM
│           ├── state.md    estado compilado — reescrito cada sesion
│           ├── log.md      historial append-only de sesiones
│           ├── index.md    catalogo de todas las paginas del wiki
│           └── sources/    documentos para que el LLM ingiera
├── areas/                  responsabilidades continuas, no proyectos
├── resources/              links y referencias
├── daily/                  logs diarios narrativos
└── .mempunk/
    ├── mempunk.db          base de datos SQLite — no editar manualmente
    └── hooks.log           log de ejecucion de hooks del ciclo de vida
```

`wiki/state.md` es el diferencial central. Es el *estado compilado* del proyecto — lo que es verdad ahora, no lo que paso en orden. El LLM lo reescribe al final de cada sesion. Leer un archivo compilado es mas rapido y preciso que leer N session logs. Cada sesion lo hace mas preciso. Cada fuente que agregas lo enriquece. Nunca lo escribes tu mismo.

## Flujo de Sesion

### Inicio de sesion

**Claude Code (modo automatico):** si activaste `auto-start` y el directorio esta vinculado a un proyecto (`project activate <id> --here`), la sesion se abre con el bloque `mempunk context` de ese proyecto ya cargado, sin agente ni preguntas. Para cambiar o crear un proyecto, usa `/mempunk:load` (plugin); sin el plugin, sigue el protocolo manual de abajo.

**Manual (sin plugin / Antigravity CLI / opencode):** sigue `vault-skills/session-start.md`. El asistente:

1. Ejecuta `mempunk project activate <id>` para establecer el proyecto activo
2. Ejecuta `mempunk session last <project_id>` para saber que hizo la sesion anterior
3. Ejecuta `mempunk skill list <project_id>` y lee todos los archivos de skills relevantes
4. Lee el estado del proyecto — `wiki/state.md` si existe, si no los ultimos 3 session log entries
5. Ejecuta `mempunk backlog list <project_id> --status pending`
6. Confirma el contexto antes de continuar

### Saves incrementales (durante la sesion)

El asistente guarda contexto inmediatamente cuando ocurre — no solo al final de la sesion:

- **Decision arquitectural tomada** → `mempunk decision add` inmediatamente
- **Bug importante resuelto** → `mempunk session log` con el resumen del fix
- **Tarea completada o iniciada** → `mempunk backlog update` inmediatamente
- **Skill del proyecto modificado** → `mempunk skill update` inmediatamente
- **Link o referencia relevante capturada** → `mempunk resource add` inmediatamente
- **Bloque de trabajo importante terminado** → `mempunk daily log` con resumen del bloque

Si la sesion se interrumpe, el contexto importante ya esta persistido.

### Fin de sesion (`vault-skills/session-end.md`)

Al terminar una sesion, el asistente:

1. Ejecuta `mempunk backlog update` por cada tarea que cambio de estado en la sesion
2. Ejecuta `mempunk decision add` por cada decision importante no guardada aun
3. Ejecuta `mempunk session log` con un resumen y la lista de archivos tocados
4. Actualiza `wiki/state.md` — lo reescribe como sintesis compilada del estado actual del proyecto
5. Agrega al `wiki/log.md`
6. Crea o agrega al `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`

La siguiente sesion retoma exactamente donde esta termino.

## Hooks del Ciclo de Vida (Claude Code)

Cuando los hooks estan instalados (`mempunk hooks install`), Mempunk responde automaticamente a los eventos de sesion de Claude Code:

| Hook | Evento | Comportamiento |
|------|--------|---------------|
| `on-prompt.js` | Antes de cada turno | Cuenta el turno y guarda el prompt en el estado de la sesión (`.mempunk/sessions/<session_id>.json`) |
| `on-tool.js` | Después de Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit y Bash | Registra en el estado de la sesión los archivos editados de verdad y los comandos corridos |
| `on-stop.js` | Despues de cada respuesta | **AutoCheckpoint** — guarda un checkpoint incremental cada 5 turnos desde el estado de la sesión, sin leer el transcript |
| `on-compact.js` | Antes de compactacion de contexto | **CompactGuard** — guarda el estado de la sesión (mensajes recientes, archivos editados, comandos) como snapshot antes de que Claude compacte |
| `on-start.js` | Inicio de sesion | **CompactRestore** — restaura el contexto desde el ultimo snapshot tras una compactacion; antes ejecuta `mempunk pull` (límite de 45 s) si `remote set --auto` está activo |
| `on-end.js` | Fin de sesión | **AutoPush** — si `remote set --auto` está activo, lanza `mempunk push --background` desacoplado y vuelve al instante. El resultado queda en `.mempunk/last-push.json`; el siguiente inicio de sesión avisa una vez si falló. Es una red de seguridad: el push del agente (`@mempunk-syncer` o `mempunk push`) escribe el commit con un resumen real |

Los dos hooks de sincronización se registran con `timeout: 90` en `settings.json`. Si `pull`/`push` falla, al contexto de Claude solo llega un mensaje fijo clasificado (red / autenticación / tiempo límite / conflicto); los detalles van a `.mempunk/hooks.log`.

El intervalo de AutoCheckpoint se puede configurar con la variable de entorno `MEMPUNK_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL` (por defecto: 5).

Los hooks tambien instalan una integracion de **statusline** — una barra de contexto en tiempo real en la barra de estado de Claude Code:

```
🟢 ███░░░░░░ 32% | claude-sonnet | $0.12
```

El emoji indica el nivel de presion: 🟢 por debajo del 70%, ⚠️ en 70–80%, 🔶 en 80–84%, 🚨 por encima del 84%.

Para recuperar contexto de una sesion anterior o tras una interrupcion:

```bash
mempunk session recover <project_id>     # ver el ultimo snapshot disponible
mempunk session checkpoints <project_id> # listar todos los checkpoints guardados
```

## Agentes (Claude Code)

Se instalan dos sub-agentes junto con los hooks (o vienen con el plugin):

| Agente | Modelo | Proposito |
|--------|--------|-----------|
| `@mempunk-recover` | Sonnet | Recupera el contexto de una sesion cerrada o interrumpida manualmente |
| `@mempunk-syncer` | Haiku (background) | Sube o baja el vault de su remote git con `mempunk push` / `mempunk pull`; el resumen va por stdin, nunca en la linea de comandos |

Con `auto-start` activado (`mempunk auto-start on`), SessionStart inyecta `mempunk context` del proyecto vinculado al directorio actual; un directorio sin vincular, o un fallo del CLI, recibe un aviso de una linea para usar `/mempunk:load`. Los guardados usan las herramientas MCP (`save_decision`, `log_session`, `backlog_update`, `update_state`).

Desde la 2.7.0 se retiran `@mempunk-loader` y `@mempunk-saver`: `mempunk hooks install`, `uninstall` y `migrate` borran las copias viejas que llevan el marcador de Mempunk.

## Servidor MCP

`mempunk mcp` es un servidor MCP local por stdio: cada CLI de IA lo lanza como subproceso al abrir la sesión. Sin red ni hosting. Expone el vault como herramientas tipadas sobre el mismo código que usa el CLI:

| Herramienta | Para qué |
|-------------|----------|
| `get_context` | Cargar el contexto compilado del proyecto (estado, última sesión, backlog pendiente, decisiones) |
| `save_decision` | Guardar un ADR en cuanto se acuerda una decisión técnica |
| `log_session` | Registrar el resumen de la sesión con los archivos tocados |
| `backlog_list` / `backlog_add` / `backlog_update` | Leer y cambiar tareas del backlog |
| `search` | Búsqueda full-text en decisiones, resources, logs diarios y logs de sesión |
| `update_state` | Reescribir `wiki/state.md` (el estado anterior pasa a su historial) |

`project_id` es opcional: por defecto el servidor usa el proyecto vinculado al directorio de la sesión (`mempunk project activate <id> --here`) o `CLAUDE_PROJECT_ID`. Nunca cae al proyecto activo global, para no guardar una decisión en el proyecto equivocado; sin vínculo, la herramienta devuelve un error que pide el `project_id`. Push y pull no se exponen: siguen siendo comandos de terminal.

Regístralo una vez por CLI. En macOS y Linux el comando es `mempunk mcp`. **En Windows**, lanza el script con `node`: los CLIs arrancan el servidor sin shell, y el shim `mempunk` (o `cmd /c mempunk mcp`) falla o agota el tiempo de espera. Obtén la ruta del script con `npm root -g`; es `<npm root -g>/mempunk/src/cli.js` (por ejemplo `C:/Users/<you>/AppData/Roaming/npm/node_modules/mempunk/src/cli.js`). Más abajo, `<cli.js>` representa esa ruta.

- **Claude Code:**
  ```bash
  claude mcp add --scope user mempunk -- mempunk mcp            # macOS / Linux
  claude mcp add --scope user mempunk -- node <cli.js> mcp      # Windows
  ```
  Compruébalo con `claude mcp list` (`mempunk: … ✔ Connected`) o con `/mcp` dentro de una sesión. Desde v2.5 lo declara el plugin.
- **opencode** (esquema de configuración v2, servidores bajo `mcp.servers`):
  ```bash
  opencode mcp add --global mempunk -- mempunk mcp              # macOS / Linux
  opencode mcp add --global mempunk -- node <cli.js> mcp        # Windows
  ```
  Esto escribe `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`:
  ```jsonc
  { "mcp": { "servers": { "mempunk": { "type": "local", "command": ["node", "<cli.js>", "mcp"] } } } }
  ```
  Compruébalo desde la carpeta de un proyecto con `opencode mcp list` (`✓ mempunk connected`), o con `/mcps` dentro de una sesión. opencode 1.x usaba en su lugar `"mcp": { "mempunk": { …, "enabled": true } }`.
- **Antigravity CLI (`agy`):**
  ```bash
  agy mcp add mempunk mempunk mcp                               # macOS / Linux
  agy mcp add mempunk node <cli.js> mcp                         # Windows
  ```
  Esto escribe `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` (`mcpServers.mempunk`). Reinicia `agy` y abre `/mcp`. En modo print (`agy -p`), las llamadas MCP necesitan una regla de permiso como `mcp(*)` en `permissions.allow`. `mempunk link --cli agy` (y `setup` en la opción 2) lo hace por ti, y además añade el vault y los protocolos de sesión a `~/.gemini/config/AGENTS.md`.
- **Gemini CLI** (ya sin mantenimiento upstream; mejor usa Antigravity CLI): añade `{ "mcpServers": { "mempunk": { "command": "mempunk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }` a `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Gemini descarta las variables de entorno que no declares: con un vault propio añade `"env": { "MEMPUNK_VAULT": "$MEMPUNK_VAULT" }`.

El servidor resuelve el proyecto a partir del directorio donde se abrió el CLI, así que abre la sesión dentro de un repositorio vinculado o pasa `project_id`. El [MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector) es útil para probar las herramientas sin un CLI: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node <cli.js> mcp`, y luego *Tools → List Tools*.

Si el vault necesita `mempunk vault upgrade`, las herramientas devuelven ese error en vez de migrar.

## Privacidad

El vault es una memoria de tu trabajo, así que en modo `full` (el predeterminado) los hooks guardan comandos y extractos de conversación, y la base de datos viaja con `mempunk push`.

- **Los secretos se ocultan al capturarlos.** Los hooks cambian el valor y conservan el contexto: `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2` se guarda como `DB_PASSWORD=[REDACTED]`. Cubre formatos conocidos de claves de API, claves privadas, JWT, URLs con credenciales, cabeceras de autorización y asignaciones tipo `password=…`.
- **Es de mejor esfuerzo.** Una contraseña sin un nombre al lado no se detecta. Decisiones, estado, registros de sesión, backlog, daily y resources también se filtran; skills y agentes no, porque son archivos que se instalan. El texto guardado por versiones anteriores sigue igual, también en el historial de git.
- **Usa un repositorio privado.** `mempunk remote set` avisa si el remote se puede leer sin credenciales.
- **Para no guardar nada de la conversación,** ejecuta `mempunk auto-session minimal`.

## Mantenimiento del Vault

```bash
# Verificar consistencia entre archivos en disco y la base de datos
mempunk sync

# Verificar integridad del vault — archivos faltantes, archivos sin registro
mempunk doctor

# Ver version del schema del vault y version del CLI
mempunk vault version

# Aplicar migraciones de schema pendientes
mempunk vault upgrade
```

`mempunk vault upgrade` es seguro de ejecutar en cualquier momento. Solo aplica migraciones pendientes y nunca modifica datos existentes.

## Como se Compara

| | Mempunk | RAG / subida de archivos | Notas manuales | Engram |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Persiste entre sesiones | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| El conocimiento se acumula | ✔ | ✘ | Depende | ✔ |
| El LLM hace el mantenimiento | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Funciona offline, sin infraestructura | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Multi-CLI | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Guarda contexto durante la sesion | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Sobrevive compactaciones de contexto | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Markdown legible (Obsidian) | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✘ |
| Sincronización por git entre máquinas | ✔ | ✘ | Depende | ✔ |

**vs RAG / subida de archivos:** Herramientas como NotebookLM o la subida de archivos de ChatGPT recuperan desde documentos en crudo en el momento de la consulta. Nada se acumula. Haz la misma pregunta dos veces y el LLM hace el mismo trabajo dos veces. Mempunk compila contexto incrementalmente — cada sesion produce un snapshot mas rico y preciso.

**vs notas manuales:** Un wiki que escribes tu mismo funciona — hasta que la carga de mantenimiento lo mata. Actualizar referencias cruzadas entre decenas de paginas es tedioso. La gente abandona los wikis porque el costo de mantenimiento crece mas rapido que el valor. Mempunk delega todo eso al LLM.

**vs Engram:** Engram es un binario de Go con SQLite + FTS5, expuesto por MCP, CLI, API HTTP y una TUI. Funciona con cualquier agente MCP (Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Codex, Antigravity…), recupera el contexto tras una compactación y se sincroniza por git. La diferencia está en el almacenamiento: Engram guarda las memorias solo en SQLite, sin capa legible por humanos. Mempunk mantiene markdown como la capa humana — decisiones, backlog, logs de sesión y un `wiki/state.md` compilado — con SQLite como backend estructurado, así que el vault se lee en cualquier editor de texto y funciona como vault de Obsidian. Una contrapartida: el sync de Engram exporta fragmentos que solo se añaden, mientras que Mempunk versiona el archivo SQLite, de modo que un conflicto entre dos máquinas aparta la base de una de ellas a un backup.

# Mempunk

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/mempunk)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mempunk)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/mempunk)](LICENSE)

Memoire persistante entre les sessions Claude Code.

## Le Probleme

Les CLI d'IA n'ont aucune memoire entre les sessions. A chaque nouvelle conversation, votre assistant ne sait pas:

- Sur quoi vous travailliez hier
- Quelles decisions d'architecture ont deja ete prises
- Quelles taches sont en attente ou terminees
- Quels fichiers ont ete modifies et pourquoi
- Quelles etaient les prochaines etapes
- Quel outil CLI vous utilisiez (Claude Code? opencode? gemini-cli?)

Vous finissez par repeter le contexte, re-expliquer les decisions et perdre l'elan. Plus le projet est long, pire c'est.

Mais il y a un probleme plus profond: meme si un CLI *se souvenait* de tout, l'historique brut est un contexte inefficace. Lire 20 session logs pour comprendre ou en est un projet est presque aussi lent que de repartir de zero. Ce dont vous avez besoin n'est pas un journal — c'est un etat compile qui devient plus precis avec le temps, pas une pile d'entrees qui ne fait que croitre.

De plus, si vous alternez entre differents CLI d'IA — Claude Code pour certains projets, opencode ou gemini-cli pour d'autres — chaque outil vit dans son propre silo. Votre contexte est fragmente entre les outils.

## La Solution

Mempunk donne a votre IA un vault structure adosse a SQLite et des fichiers markdown — et le maintient compile, pas seulement stocke.

- **Debut de session** (`vault-skills/session-start.md`): l'assistant charge l'etat compile du projet depuis `wiki/state.md` s'il existe, ou les derniers session logs sinon. Sans re-expliquer. Sans re-deriver. Il reprend la ou vous vous etiez arrete.
- **Fin de session** (`vault-skills/session-end.md`): l'assistant ecrit le session log, met a jour le backlog et recrit l'etat compile — une synthese fraiche de tout ce qui s'est passe jusqu'ici. La session suivante demarre avec un snapshot dense et precis plutot qu'un historique brut.
- **Le vault** (toujours): chaque projet accumule un `wiki/` — une base de connaissances que le LLM construit et maintient. Chaque session le rend plus precis. Chaque source que vous ajoutez l'enrichit.

Le vault est constitue de fichiers markdown organises par projet, avec SQLite comme backend structure. Vous le gerez avec un CLI. Votre assistant IA le navigue avec les protocoles definis dans `vault-skills/`. Il fonctionne aussi comme vault Obsidian, pour naviguer et chercher tout visuellement.

Comme le vault est agnostique au CLI, vous pouvez utiliser le même vault avec Claude Code, opencode et Antigravity CLI (via le serveur MCP) simultanément. Changez de CLI sans perdre le contexte.

## Installation

**Prérequis :** Node.js 22 ou supérieur, et au moins un CLI de programmation IA (Claude Code, opencode ou Antigravity CLI). Git n'est nécessaire que pour [synchroniser le vault entre machines](README.md#sync-between-machines).

### 1. Installer le CLI

```bash
npm install -g mempunk
mempunk -v
```

### 2. Créer le vault et lier votre CLI

```bash
mempunk setup
```

`setup` pose deux questions :

1. **Quel CLI IA utilisez-vous principalement ?** `1` pour Claude Code, `2` pour opencode ou un autre CLI.
2. **(Claude Code uniquement) Comment Mempunk doit-il fonctionner ?** `1` *Automatique* (recommandé) installe les hooks, les agents et la status line, et active `auto-start`. `2` *Manuel* n'installe que les protocoles vault-skills, que vous suivez vous-même.

Il crée `~/Dev-Brain/`, l'ajoute aux répertoires de votre CLI et installe les hooks + agents (Claude Code, automatique) ou les protocoles `vault-skills/` (manuel, opencode). Le relancer est sans risque : il conserve le vault existant. Définissez `MEMPUNK_VAULT` avant de le lancer pour utiliser un autre emplacement.

#### Claude Code : plugin ou hooks manuels

Avec Claude Code, vous pouvez utiliser Mempunk comme plugin au lieu d'installer des hooks dans `~/.claude` :

```bash
mempunk setup --plugin
```

Cela exécute `claude plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` et `claude plugin install mempunk@mempunk`. Si `claude` est absent ou échoue, `setup` revient aux hooks manuels. Vous pouvez aussi lancer ces deux commandes vous-même, ou utiliser `/plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` puis `/plugin install mempunk@mempunk` dans Claude Code.

- **Le plugin a toujours besoin du CLI.** Il ne contient aucun code de hook : il trouve votre `mempunk` installé et exécute ses hooks, donc `npm update -g mempunk` les met aussi à jour.
- **Vous utilisez déjà des hooks manuels ?** Lancez d'abord `mempunk hooks migrate`. Avec le plugin actif, les hooks manuels ne s'exécutent pas : rien ne tourne deux fois.
- **Barre d'état.** Un plugin ne peut pas la configurer : lancez `mempunk statusline install`.
- **Volta ou préfixe personnalisé.** Si le plugin signale qu'il ne trouve pas le CLI, définissez `MEMPUNK_CLI="node <chemin du paquet>/src/cli.js"`.

### 3. Enregistrer votre premier projet

Depuis la racine de votre dépôt :

```bash
cd ~/code/my-api
mempunk project add api "Backend API"
```

L'id (`api`) est celui que vous utilisez dans toutes les autres commandes. `project add` associe le répertoire courant au projet, de sorte que les sessions ouvertes à cet endroit le résolvent automatiquement. Pour un projet qui existe déjà (autre dossier, autre machine), liez le dossier avec `mempunk project activate api --here`.

### 4. Connecter le serveur MCP (recommandé)

Le serveur MCP donne à l'assistant des outils typés (`get_context`, `save_decision`, `search`…) au lieu de commandes shell. Enregistrez-le une fois par CLI comme indiqué dans [Serveur MCP](#serveur-mcp).

### 5. Vérifier l'installation

```bash
mempunk status                # vault, projets, dernière session
mempunk hooks install --check # Claude Code : hooks, agents et status line
mempunk doctor                # intégrité du vault
```

Ouvrez une session de votre CLI dans le dossier du projet. Avec Claude Code en mode automatique, le bloc de contexte est déjà là au démarrage de la session.

## Utilisation

Une journée type avec un projet :

1. **Ouvrez votre CLI dans le dépôt.** Avec `auto-start` activé, Claude Code démarre avec le contexte compilé du projet (état, dernière session, backlog en attente, décisions récentes). Sinon, tapez `/mempunk` ou demandez à l'assistant de charger le contexte Mempunk : il liste vos projets et demande sur lequel travailler.
2. **Travaillez normalement.** L'assistant sauvegarde au fil de l'eau : une décision dès qu'elle est convenue, une mise à jour du backlog quand une tâche démarre ou se termine, une ressource quand vous partagez un lien. Vous pouvez aussi le lui demander directement (« enregistre ceci comme décision », « ajoute-le au backlog »), ou lancer les commandes vous-même :
   ```bash
   mempunk decision add api "Use JWT for auth" --tags "auth"
   mempunk backlog add api "Add refresh tokens" --priority 1
   mempunk search "refresh token" --project api
   ```
3. **Fermez la session.** Tapez `/session-end` ou dites à l'assistant que vous avez terminé. Il enregistre la session, met à jour le backlog et réécrit `wiki/state.md`, pour que la session suivante démarre d'un snapshot compilé plutôt que de l'historique brut.
4. **Vous changez de machine ?** `mempunk push` avant de partir et `mempunk pull` sur l'autre machine (ou `mempunk remote set <url> --auto` pour que les hooks fassent les deux).

Si une session se ferme de manière inattendue, `mempunk session recover api` affiche le dernier snapshot automatique.

## Structure du Vault

```
~/Dev-Brain/
├── projects/
│   └── <id>/
│       ├── INDEX.md        metadonnees (nom, created_at, status)
│       ├── decisions/      architecture decision records (ADRs)
│       ├── skills/         stack, patterns, conventions — charges a chaque session
│       └── wiki/           base de connaissances maintenue par le LLM
│           ├── state.md    etat compile — recrit a chaque session
│           ├── log.md      historique append-only des sessions
│           ├── index.md    catalogue de toutes les pages du wiki
│           └── sources/    documents a faire ingerer par le LLM
├── areas/                  responsabilites continues, pas des projets
├── resources/              liens et references
├── daily/                  logs journaliers narratifs
└── .mempunk/
    ├── mempunk.db          base de donnees SQLite — ne pas modifier manuellement
    └── hooks.log           journal d'execution des hooks du cycle de vie
```

`wiki/state.md` est le differenciateur central. C'est l'*etat compile* du projet — ce qui est vrai maintenant, pas ce qui s'est passe dans l'ordre. Le LLM le recrit a la fin de chaque session. Lire un fichier compile est plus rapide et plus precis que lire N session logs. Chaque session le rend plus precis. Chaque source que vous ajoutez l'enrichit. Vous ne l'ecrivez jamais vous-meme.

## Flux de Session

### Debut de session

**Claude Code (mode automatique):** si vous avez active `auto-start` et que le repertoire est lie a un projet (`project activate <id> --here`), la session s'ouvre avec le bloc `mempunk context` de ce projet deja charge, sans agent ni questions. Pour changer ou creer un projet, utilisez `/mempunk:load` (plugin) ; sans le plugin, suivez le protocole manuel ci-dessous.

**Manuel (sans plugin / Antigravity CLI / opencode):** suivez `vault-skills/session-start.md`. L'assistant:

1. Execute `mempunk project activate <id>` pour definir le projet actif
2. Execute `mempunk session last <project_id>` pour savoir ce que la session precedente a fait
3. Execute `mempunk skill list <project_id>` et lit tous les fichiers de skill pertinents
4. Lit l'etat du projet — `wiki/state.md` si existant, sinon les 3 derniers session log entries
5. Execute `mempunk backlog list <project_id> --status pending`
6. Confirme le contexte avant de continuer

### Saves incrementaux (pendant la session)

L'assistant sauvegarde le contexte immediatement quand cela se produit — pas seulement en fin de session:

- **Decision architecturale prise** → `mempunk decision add` immediatement
- **Bug important resolu** → `mempunk session log` avec le resume du correctif
- **Tache completee ou demarree** → `mempunk backlog update` immediatement
- **Skill du projet modifie** → `mempunk skill update` immediatement
- **Lien ou reference pertinente capture** → `mempunk resource add` immediatement
- **Bloc de travail important termine** → `mempunk daily log` avec resume du bloc

Si une session est interrompue, le contexte important est deja persiste.

### Fin de session (`vault-skills/session-end.md`)

Quand une session se termine, l'assistant:

1. Execute `mempunk backlog update` pour chaque tache qui a change de statut pendant la session
2. Execute `mempunk decision add` pour chaque decision importante pas encore sauvegardee
3. Execute `mempunk session log` avec un resume et la liste des fichiers touches
4. Met a jour `wiki/state.md` — le recrit comme synthese compilee de l'etat actuel du projet
5. Ajoute au `wiki/log.md`
6. Cree ou ajoute au `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`

La prochaine session reprend exactement la ou celle-ci s'est arretee.

## Hooks du Cycle de Vie (Claude Code)

Quand les hooks sont installes (`mempunk hooks install`), Mempunk repond automatiquement aux evenements de session de Claude Code:

| Hook | Evenement | Comportement |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| `on-prompt.js` | Avant chaque tour | Compte le tour et garde le prompt dans l'état de la session (`.mempunk/sessions/<session_id>.json`) |
| `on-tool.js` | Après Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit et Bash | Enregistre dans l'état de la session les fichiers réellement modifiés et les commandes lancées |
| `on-stop.js` | Apres chaque reponse | **AutoCheckpoint** — sauvegarde un checkpoint incremental tous les 5 tours depuis l'état de la session, sans lire le transcript |
| `on-compact.js` | Avant compaction du contexte | **CompactGuard** — sauvegarde l'état de la session (messages récents, fichiers modifiés, commandes) comme snapshot avant que Claude compacte |
| `on-start.js` | Debut de session | **CompactRestore** — restaure le contexte depuis le dernier snapshot apres une compaction ; lance d'abord `mempunk pull` (délai de 45 s) si `remote set --auto` est actif |
| `on-end.js` | Fin de session | **AutoPush** — si `remote set --auto` est actif, lance `mempunk push --background` en arrière-plan détaché et rend la main aussitôt. Le résultat va dans `.mempunk/last-push.json` ; le démarrage de session suivant avertit une fois en cas d'échec. C'est un filet de sécurité : le push de l'agent (`@mempunk-syncer` ou `mempunk push`) écrit le commit avec un vrai résumé |

Les deux hooks de synchronisation sont enregistrés avec `timeout: 90` dans `settings.json`. Si `pull`/`push` échoue, seul un message fixe classé (réseau / authentification / délai / conflit) atteint le contexte de Claude ; les détails vont dans `.mempunk/hooks.log`.

L'intervalle d'AutoCheckpoint est configurable via la variable d'environnement `MEMPUNK_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL` (defaut: 5).

Les hooks installent aussi une integration **statusline** — une barre de contexte en temps reel dans la barre de statut de Claude Code:

```
🟢 ███░░░░░░ 32% | claude-sonnet | $0.12
```

L'emoji indique le niveau de pression: 🟢 sous 70%, ⚠️ entre 70–80%, 🔶 entre 80–84%, 🚨 au-dessus de 84%.

Pour recuperer le contexte d'une session precedente ou apres une interruption:

```bash
mempunk session recover <project_id>     # voir le dernier snapshot disponible
mempunk session checkpoints <project_id> # lister tous les checkpoints sauvegardes
```

## Agents (Claude Code)

Deux sous-agents sont installes avec les hooks (ou fournis par le plugin):

| Agent | Modele | Objectif |
|-------|--------|----------|
| `@mempunk-recover` | Sonnet | Recupere le contexte d'une session fermee ou interrompue manuellement |
| `@mempunk-syncer` | Haiku (background) | Pousse ou recupere le vault depuis son remote git avec `mempunk push` / `mempunk pull` ; le resume passe par stdin, jamais par la ligne de commande |

Avec `auto-start` active (`mempunk auto-start on`), SessionStart injecte `mempunk context` du projet lie au repertoire courant ; un repertoire non lie, ou un echec du CLI, recoit un avis d'une ligne pour utiliser `/mempunk:load`. Les sauvegardes passent par les outils MCP (`save_decision`, `log_session`, `backlog_update`, `update_state`).

Depuis la 2.7.0, `@mempunk-loader` et `@mempunk-saver` sont retires : `mempunk hooks install`, `uninstall` et `migrate` suppriment les anciennes copies qui portent le marqueur de Mempunk.

## Serveur MCP

`mempunk mcp` est un serveur MCP local en stdio : chaque CLI d'IA le lance comme sous-processus a l'ouverture de la session. Pas de reseau ni d'hebergement. Il expose le vault en outils types, sur le meme code que le CLI :

| Outil | Pour |
|-------|------|
| `get_context` | Charger le contexte compile du projet (etat, derniere session, backlog en attente, decisions) |
| `save_decision` | Enregistrer un ADR des qu'une decision technique est prise |
| `log_session` | Enregistrer le resume de la session avec les fichiers touches |
| `backlog_list` / `backlog_add` / `backlog_update` | Lire et modifier les taches du backlog |
| `search` | Recherche full-text dans les decisions, resources, logs quotidiens et logs de session |
| `update_state` | Reecrire `wiki/state.md` (l'etat precedent passe dans son historique) |

`project_id` est optionnel : par defaut le serveur utilise le projet lie au repertoire de la session (`mempunk project activate <id> --here`) ou `CLAUDE_PROJECT_ID`. Il ne se rabat jamais sur le projet actif global ; sans lien, l'outil renvoie une erreur qui demande `project_id`. Push et pull ne sont pas exposes.

À enregistrer une fois par CLI. Sur macOS et Linux, la commande est `mempunk mcp`. **Sous Windows**, lancez le script avec `node` : les CLI démarrent le serveur sans shell, et le shim `mempunk` (ou `cmd /c mempunk mcp`) échoue ou dépasse le délai d'attente. Trouvez le chemin du script avec `npm root -g` ; c'est `<npm root -g>/mempunk/src/cli.js` (par exemple `C:/Users/<you>/AppData/Roaming/npm/node_modules/mempunk/src/cli.js`). Ci-dessous, `<cli.js>` désigne ce chemin.

- **Claude Code :**
  ```bash
  claude mcp add --scope user mempunk -- mempunk mcp            # macOS / Linux
  claude mcp add --scope user mempunk -- node <cli.js> mcp      # Windows
  ```
  Vérifiez-le avec `claude mcp list` (`mempunk: … ✔ Connected`) ou `/mcp` dans une session. À partir de v2.5, le plugin le déclare pour vous.
- **opencode** (schéma de configuration v2, serveurs sous `mcp.servers`) :
  ```bash
  opencode mcp add --global mempunk -- mempunk mcp              # macOS / Linux
  opencode mcp add --global mempunk -- node <cli.js> mcp        # Windows
  ```
  Cela écrit `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` :
  ```jsonc
  { "mcp": { "servers": { "mempunk": { "type": "local", "command": ["node", "<cli.js>", "mcp"] } } } }
  ```
  Vérifiez-le depuis un dossier de projet avec `opencode mcp list` (`✓ mempunk connected`), ou `/mcps` dans une session. opencode 1.x utilisait `"mcp": { "mempunk": { …, "enabled": true } }` à la place.
- **Antigravity CLI (`agy`) :**
  ```bash
  agy mcp add mempunk mempunk mcp                               # macOS / Linux
  agy mcp add mempunk node <cli.js> mcp                         # Windows
  ```
  Cela écrit `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` (`mcpServers.mempunk`). Redémarrez `agy` et ouvrez `/mcp`. En mode print (`agy -p`), les appels MCP nécessitent une règle d'autorisation comme `mcp(*)` sous `permissions.allow`. `mempunk link --cli agy` (et `setup` avec l'option 2) le fait pour vous, et ajoute aussi le vault et les protocoles de session à `~/.gemini/config/AGENTS.md`.
- **Gemini CLI** (plus maintenu en amont ; préférez Antigravity CLI) : ajoutez `{ "mcpServers": { "mempunk": { "command": "mempunk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }` à `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Gemini supprime les variables d'environnement non déclarées : avec un vault personnalisé, ajoutez `"env": { "MEMPUNK_VAULT": "$MEMPUNK_VAULT" }`.

Le serveur résout le projet à partir du répertoire dans lequel le CLI a été ouvert : ouvrez donc la session dans un dépôt lié ou passez `project_id`. Le [MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector) est pratique pour essayer les outils sans CLI : `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node <cli.js> mcp`, puis *Tools → List Tools*.

Si le vault a besoin de `mempunk vault upgrade`, les outils renvoient cette erreur au lieu de migrer.

## Confidentialité

Le vault est une mémoire de votre travail : en mode `full` (par défaut), les hooks stockent donc des commandes et des extraits de conversation, et la base de données voyage avec `mempunk push`.

- **Les secrets sont masqués à la capture.** Les hooks remplacent la valeur et gardent le contexte : `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2` est stocké comme `DB_PASSWORD=[REDACTED]`. Cela couvre les formats connus de clés d'API, les clés privées, les JWT, les URL avec identifiants, les en-têtes d'autorisation et les affectations du type `password=…`.
- **Ce filtrage n'est pas garanti.** Un mot de passe sans nom à côté n'est pas détecté. Les décisions, l'état, les journaux de session, le backlog, les daily et les ressources sont aussi filtrés ; pas les skills ni les agents, qui sont des fichiers installés. Le texte enregistré par les versions précédentes reste inchangé, y compris dans l'historique git.
- **Utilisez un dépôt privé.** `mempunk remote set` vous avertit si le remote est lisible sans identifiants.
- **Pour ne stocker aucun texte de conversation,** lancez `mempunk auto-session minimal`.

## Maintenance du Vault

```bash
# Verifier la coherence entre les fichiers sur disque et la base de donnees
mempunk sync

# Verifier l'integrite du vault — fichiers manquants, fichiers non enregistres
mempunk doctor

# Afficher la version du schema du vault et la version du CLI
mempunk vault version

# Appliquer les migrations de schema en attente
mempunk vault upgrade
```

`mempunk vault upgrade` est sans risque a tout moment. Il n'applique que les migrations manquantes et ne modifie jamais les donnees existantes.

**vs notes manuelles:** Un wiki que vous ecrivez vous-meme fonctionne — jusqu'a ce que le fardeau de maintenance le tue. Mettre a jour les references croisees sur des dizaines de pages est fastidieux. Les gens abandonnent les wikis parce que le cout de maintenance croit plus vite que la valeur. # Mempunk

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/mempunk)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mempunk)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/mempunk)](LICENSE)

Persistent memory between Claude Code sessions.

## The Problem

AI coding CLIs have no memory between sessions. Every time you start a new conversation, your assistant doesn't know:

- What you were working on yesterday
- What architectural decisions were already made
- What tasks are pending or done
- What files were modified and why
- What the next steps were supposed to be
- Which CLI tool you were using (Claude Code? opencode? gemini-cli?)

You end up repeating context, re-explaining decisions, and losing momentum. The longer a project runs, the worse it gets.

But there's a deeper issue: even if a CLI *did* remember everything, raw history is inefficient context. Reading 20 session logs to understand where a project stands is nearly as slow as starting from scratch. What you need isn't a log — it's a compiled state that gets more accurate over time, not a pile of entries that keeps growing.

On top of that, if you switch between different AI coding CLIs — Claude Code for some projects, opencode or gemini-cli for others — each tool lives in its own silo. Your context is fragmented across tools.

## The Solution

Mempunk gives your AI a structured vault backed by SQLite and markdown files — and keeps it compiled, not just stored.

- **Session start** (`vault-skills/session-start.md`): the assistant loads the compiled project state from `wiki/state.md` if it exists, or the last session logs otherwise. No re-explaining. No re-deriving. It picks up where you left off.
- **Session end** (`vault-skills/session-end.md`): the assistant writes the session log, updates the backlog, and rewrites the compiled state — a fresh synthesis of everything that's happened so far. The next session starts with a dense, accurate snapshot instead of raw history.
- **The vault** (always): each project accumulates a `wiki/` — a knowledge base the LLM owns and maintains. Every session makes it more accurate. Every source you add makes it richer.

The vault is markdown files organized by project, with SQLite as the structured backend. You manage it with a CLI. Your AI navigates it with the protocols defined in `vault-skills/`. It also works as an Obsidian vault, so you can browse and search everything visually.

Because the vault is CLI-agnostic, you can use the same vault with Claude Code, opencode, and Antigravity CLI (through the MCP server) simultaneously. Switch between CLIs without losing context.

## Installation

**Requirements:** Node.js 22 or later, and at least one AI coding CLI (Claude Code, opencode or Antigravity CLI). Git is only needed to [sync the vault between machines](#sync-between-machines).

### 1. Install the CLI

```bash
npm install -g mempunk
mempunk -v
```

### 2. Create the vault and link your CLI

```bash
mempunk setup
```

`setup` asks two questions:

1. **Which AI CLI do you mainly use?** `1` for Claude Code, `2` for opencode or another CLI.
2. **(Claude Code only) How should Mempunk work?** `1` *Automatic* (recommended) installs hooks, agents and the status line, and turns on `auto-start`. `2` *Manual* installs only the vault-skills protocols, which you follow yourself.

It creates `~/Dev-Brain/`, adds it to your CLI's directories, and installs hooks + agents (Claude Code, automatic) or the `vault-skills/` protocols (manual, opencode). Running it again is safe: it keeps the existing vault. Set `MEMPUNK_VAULT` before running it to use a different location.

#### Claude Code: plugin or manual hooks

With Claude Code you can run Mempunk as a plugin instead of installing hooks into `~/.claude`:

```bash
mempunk setup --plugin
```

This runs `claude plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` and `claude plugin install mempunk@mempunk`. If `claude` is missing or fails, `setup` falls back to manual hooks. You can also run those two commands yourself, or use `/plugin marketplace add JuanesEspinosa/Mempunk` and then `/plugin install mempunk@mempunk` inside Claude Code.

- **The plugin still needs the CLI.** It ships no hook code: it finds your installed `mempunk` and runs its hooks, so `npm update -g mempunk` updates them too.
- **Already using manual hooks?** Run `mempunk hooks migrate` first. With the plugin active, manual hooks don't run, so nothing fires twice.
- **Status line.** A plugin can't set it: run `mempunk statusline install`.
- **Volta or a custom prefix.** If the plugin warns that it can't find the CLI, set `MEMPUNK_CLI="node <package path>/src/cli.js"`.

### 3. Register your first project

From the root of your repository:

```bash
cd ~/code/my-api
mempunk project add api "Backend API"
```

The id (`api`) is what you use in every other command. `project add` maps the current directory to the project, so sessions opened there resolve it automatically. For a project that already exists (another folder, another machine), link the folder with `mempunk project activate api --here`.

### 4. Connect the MCP server (recommended)

The MCP server gives the assistant typed tools (`get_context`, `save_decision`, `search`…) instead of shell commands. Register it once per CLI as shown in [MCP server](#mcp-server).

### 5. Check the installation

```bash
mempunk status                # vault, projects, last session
mempunk hooks install --check # Claude Code: hooks, agents and status line
mempunk doctor                # vault integrity
```

Open a session of your CLI in the project folder. With Claude Code in automatic mode, the context block is already there when the session starts.

## Usage

A typical day with a project:

1. **Open your CLI in the repository.** With `auto-start` on, Claude Code starts with the project's compiled context (state, last session, pending backlog, recent decisions). Otherwise type `/mempunk`, or ask the assistant to load the Mempunk context: it lists your projects and asks which one to work on.
2. **Work as usual.** The assistant saves as things happen: a decision when one is agreed, a backlog update when a task starts or ends, a resource when you share a link. You can also ask it directly ("save this as a decision", "add it to the backlog"), or run the commands yourself:
   ```bash
   mempunk decision add api "Use JWT for auth" --tags "auth"
   mempunk backlog add api "Add refresh tokens" --priority 1
   mempunk search "refresh token" --project api
   ```
3. **Close the session.** Type `/session-end` or tell the assistant you are done. It logs the session, updates the backlog, and rewrites `wiki/state.md`, so the next session starts from a compiled snapshot instead of raw history.
4. **Switching machines?** `mempunk push` before you leave and `mempunk pull` on the other machine (or `mempunk remote set <url> --auto` to do both from the hooks).

If a session closes unexpectedly, `mempunk session recover api` shows the last automatic snapshot.

## Vault Structure

```
~/Dev-Brain/
├── projects/
│   └── <id>/
│       ├── INDEX.md        metadata (name, created_at, status)
│       ├── decisions/      architecture decision records (ADRs)
│       ├── skills/         stack, patterns, conventions — loaded each session
│       └── wiki/           LLM-maintained knowledge base
│           ├── state.md    compiled project state — rewritten each session
│           ├── log.md      append-only session history
│           ├── index.md    catalog of all wiki pages
│           └── sources/    documents for the LLM to ingest
├── areas/                  ongoing responsibilities, not projects
├── resources/              links and references
├── daily/                  narrative daily logs
└── .mempunk/
    ├── mempunk.db          SQLite database — do not edit manually
    └── hooks.log           lifecycle hook execution log
```

`wiki/state.md` is the central differentiator. It's the *compiled state* of the project — what's true now, not what happened in order. The LLM rewrites it at the end of every session. Reading one compiled file is faster and more accurate than reading N session logs. Every session makes it more precise. Every source you add enriches it. You never write it yourself.

## Session Flow

### Session start

**Claude Code (auto mode):** if you enabled `auto-start` and the directory is linked to a project (`project activate <id> --here`), the session opens with that project's `mempunk context` block already loaded — no agent, no questions. To switch or create a project, use `/mempunk:load` (plugin); without the plugin, follow the manual protocol below.

**Manual (no plugin / Antigravity CLI / opencode):** follow `vault-skills/session-start.md`. The assistant:

1. Runs `mempunk project activate <id>` to set the active project
2. Runs `mempunk session last <project_id>` to know what the previous session did
3. Runs `mempunk skill list <project_id>` and reads all relevant skill files
4. Reads project state — `wiki/state.md` if it exists, otherwise the last 3 session log entries
5. Runs `mempunk backlog list <project_id> --status pending`
6. Confirms context before proceeding

### Incremental saves (during session)

The assistant saves context immediately when it happens — not only at session end:

- **Architectural decision made** → `mempunk decision add` immediately
- **Important bug fixed** → `mempunk session log` with the fix summary
- **Task completed or started** → `mempunk backlog update` immediately
- **Project skill modified** → `mempunk skill update` immediately
- **Relevant link captured** → `mempunk resource add` immediately
- **Important work block finished** → `mempunk daily log` with a block summary

If a session is interrupted, the important context is already persisted.

### Session end (`vault-skills/session-end.md`)

When a session ends, the assistant:

1. Runs `mempunk backlog update` for each task that changed status during the session
2. Runs `mempunk decision add` for each important decision not yet saved
3. Runs `mempunk session log` with a summary and the list of files touched
4. Updates `wiki/state.md` — rewrites it as a compiled synthesis of the current project state
5. Appends to `wiki/log.md`
6. Creates or appends to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`

The next session picks up exactly where this one left off.

## Lifecycle Hooks (Claude Code)

When hooks are installed (`mempunk hooks install`), Mempunk automatically responds to Claude Code session events:

| Hook | Event | Behavior |
|------|-------|----------|
| `on-prompt.js` | Before each turn | Counts the turn and keeps the prompt in the session state (`.mempunk/sessions/<session_id>.json`) |
| `on-tool.js` | After Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and Bash | Records the files actually edited and the commands run in the session state |
| `on-stop.js` | After each response | **AutoCheckpoint** — saves an incremental checkpoint every 5 turns from the session state, without reading the transcript |
| `on-compact.js` | Before context compaction | **CompactGuard** — saves the session state (recent messages, edited files, commands) as a snapshot before Claude compacts |
| `on-start.js` | Session start | **CompactRestore** — restores context from the last snapshot after compaction; runs `mempunk pull` first (45 s timeout) if `remote set --auto` is on |
| `on-end.js` | Session end | **AutoPush** — if `remote set --auto` is on, launches `mempunk push --background` detached and returns at once. The result goes to `.mempunk/last-push.json`; the next session start warns once if it failed. It is a safety net: the agent's push (`@mempunk-syncer` or `mempunk push`) writes the commit with a real summary |

Both sync hooks are registered with `timeout: 90` in `settings.json`. If `pull`/`push` fails, only a fixed classified message (network / auth / timeout / conflict) reaches Claude's context; details go to `.mempunk/hooks.log`.

AutoCheckpoint interval is configurable via the `MEMPUNK_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL` environment variable (default: 5).

Hooks also install a **statusline** integration — a real-time context bar in Claude Code's status line:

```
🟢 ███░░░░░░ 32% | claude-sonnet | $0.12
```

The emoji indicates pressure level: 🟢 below 70%, ⚠️ at 70–80%, 🔶 at 80–84%, 🚨 above 84%.

To recover context from a previous session or after an interruption:

```bash
mempunk session recover <project_id>     # show latest available snapshot
mempunk session checkpoints <project_id> # list all saved checkpoints
```

## Agents (Claude Code)

Two sub-agents are installed alongside hooks (or come with the plugin):

| Agent | Model | Purpose |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `@mempunk-recover` | Sonnet | Recovers context from a closed or interrupted session manually |
| `@mempunk-syncer` | Haiku (background) | Pushes/pulls the vault to its git remote via `mempunk push` / `mempunk pull`; the summary goes through stdin, never on the command line (see [Sync between machines](#sync-between-machines)) |

With `auto-start` enabled (`mempunk auto-start on`), SessionStart injects `mempunk context` for the project linked to the current directory; an unlinked directory, or a CLI failure, gets a one-line notice to use `/mempunk:load`. Saving goes through the [MCP tools](#mcp-server) (`save_decision`, `log_session`, `backlog_update`, `update_state`).

Since 2.7.0, `@mempunk-loader` and `@mempunk-saver` are retired: `mempunk hooks install`, `uninstall` and `migrate` delete old copies that carry Mempunk's marker.

## MCP server

`mempunk mcp` is a local MCP server over stdio: each AI CLI launches it as a subprocess when a session opens. No network, no hosting. It exposes the vault as typed tools on the same code the CLI uses:

| Tool | Use it to |
|------|-----------|
| `get_context` | Load the compiled project context (state, last session, pending backlog, decisions) |
| `save_decision` | Save an ADR as soon as a technical decision is agreed |
| `log_session` | Log a session summary with the files touched |
| `backlog_list` / `backlog_add` / `backlog_update` | Read and change backlog tasks |
| `search` | Full-text search over decisions, resources, daily logs and session logs |
| `update_state` | Rewrite `wiki/state.md` (the previous state goes to its history) |

`project_id` is optional: by default the server uses the project linked to the session's directory (`mempunk project activate <id> --here`) or `CLAUDE_PROJECT_ID`. Push and pull are not exposed: they stay terminal commands.

**New machine.** Clone the vault into `~/Dev-Brain` *before* running any mempunk command there. Running `mempunk init` first and then `remote set`/`pull` fails with an "unrelated histories" error; the CLI prints a hint to clone instead.

**Remote URL.** Accepted forms: https/ssh/git/file URLs, scp-style `git@host:path`, and local paths. URLs that embed credentials (`https://user:token@…`) are rejected — use git's credential helper or SSH keys. Branch names are validated with `git check-ref-format`. `remote set` also untracks per-machine files that were previously committed (`auto-start.flag`, `hooks.log`, backups) and warns that the DB contains session snapshots with conversation excerpts, so the remote must be a **private** repository. To keep conversation text out of the DB from now on, run `mempunk auto-session minimal`.

**Commit messages.** Sources in precedence order: `--message-file <path>`, `--message-stdin` (whole message from stdin), `-m "<msg>"`, default `vault: session <YYYY-MM-DD> — <n> files`. The message is prefixed `vault(<project>):` with `--project` or `vault:` without. Messages are sanitized (control characters removed, 2000 chars max); `--project` must be a plain identifier (letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.`).

**Conflicts.** Neither command stashes: local uncommitted changes are committed first (`pull` uses `vault: local changes before pull`), then the remote branch is fetched and merged. If both machines wrote to `mempunk.db`, the DB with the most recent activity wins and the loser is saved as `.mempunk/backups/conflict-<stamp>-<ours|theirs>.db` (`--strict` exits 1 after resolving). If markdown files conflict, the command stops with the list and the merge stays in progress: resolve, then `git add`/`git commit` in `~/Dev-Brain` (or `git merge --abort`). A subsequent `push`/`pull` refuses to run while a merge is in progress or `.git/index.lock` exists. Both commands run the DB integrity check after any merge. Git runs non-interactively (`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`) with timeouts, so a missing credential fails fast instead of opening a prompt.

**Per-machine paths (vault v5).** Repo paths live in `project_paths` keyed by hostname, normalized (lowercase, `.local`/`.lan` stripped); `MEMPUNK_HOST` overrides it and is normalized the same way. `project activate <id> --here` maps the folder on this machine only, and `mempunk pull` lists the projects that still need it. Existing vaults need `mempunk vault upgrade`.

**Agent.** `@mempunk-syncer` (installed by `mempunk hooks install`) runs `mempunk push` / `mempunk pull` in the background from `SYNC push: project=<id> summary="<summary>"` or `SYNC pull:`. It sends the summary through a quoted heredoc, never on the command line:

```bash
mempunk push --project <id> --message-stdin <<'MEMPUNK_EOF'
<summary>
MEMPUNK_EOF
```

It never runs git directly and never relays raw git stderr. With no remote configured it prints `MEMPUNK-SYNCER: no remote configured — run: mempunk remote set <url>`; on failure it prints `MEMPUNK-SYNCER ERROR: mempunk push failed (exit N) — run it manually in the terminal to see details`. With `--auto`, `on-start.js` pulls at `SessionStart` and `on-end.js` pushes at `SessionEnd`.

## Privacy

The vault is a memory of your work, so in `full` mode (the default) hooks store commands and conversation excerpts, and the database travels with `mempunk push`.

- **Secrets are hidden when captured.** Hooks replace the value and keep the context: `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2` is stored as `DB_PASSWORD=[REDACTED]`. This covers known API key formats, private keys, JWTs, URLs with credentials, authorization headers and `password=…`-style assignments.
- **It is best effort.** A password with no name next to it is not detected,. Decisions, state, session logs, backlog, daily logs and resources are filtered too; skills and agents are not, because they are installed files. Text saved by earlier versions stays as it was, including in the git history.
- **Use a private repository.** `mempunk remote set` warns you if the remote can be read without credentials.
- **To store no conversation text at all,** run `mempunk auto-session minimal`.

## Vault Maintenance

```bash
# Check consistency between files on disk and the database
mempunk sync

# Check vault integrity — missing files, unregistered files
mempunk doctor

# Show vault schema version and CLI version
mempunk vault version

# Apply pending schema migrations
mempunk vault upgrade
```

`mempunk vault upgrade` is safe to run at any time. It only applies missing migrations and never modifies existing data.

| | Mempunk | RAG / file uploads | Manual notes | Engram |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Persists between sessions | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Knowledge accumulates | ✔ | ✘ | Depends | ✔ |
| LLM does the maintenance | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Works offline, no infrastructure | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Cross-CLI | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Auto-saves during session | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Survives context compaction | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Human-readable markdown (Obsidian) | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✘ |
| Git sync between machines | ✔ | ✘ | Depends | ✔ |

**vs RAG / file uploads:** Tools like NotebookLM or ChatGPT file uploads retrieve from raw documents at query time. Nothing accumulates. Ask the same question twice and the LLM does the same work twice. Mempunk compiles context incrementally — each session produces a richer, more accurate snapshot.

**vs manual notes:** A wiki you write yourself works — until the maintenance burden kills it. Updating cross-references across dozens of pages is tedious. People abandon wikis because the cost of maintenance grows faster than the value. Mempunk delegates all of that to the LLM.

**vs Engram:** Engram is a Go binary with SQLite + FTS5, exposed through MCP, a CLI, an HTTP API and a TUI. It works with any MCP agent (Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Codex, Antigravity…), recovers context after compaction and syncs through git. The difference is the storage layer: Engram keeps memories only in SQLite, with no human-readable layer. Mempunk keeps markdown as the human layer — decisions, backlog, session logs and a compiled `wiki/state.md` — with SQLite as the structured backend, so the vault is readable in any text editor and works as an Obsidian vault. One trade-off: Engram's git sync exports append-only chunks, while Mempunk versions the SQLite file, so a conflict between two machines sets one machine's database aside as a backup.
